title: UX Ideas That Do More Harm Than Good
intro: Across three articles in three years, Calabro returns to the same list: useful ideas that get misused as shortcuts. Each has a real meaning and a rule of thumb that keeps it honest.

topics.title: UX Ideas That Do More Harm Than Good

learn.title: Four ideas and their alibi versions
learn.text:
**Aesthetic-usability effect** — attractive interfaces are *perceived* as easier (Kurosu & Kashimura). The original research noted the effect is modest and varies across cultures. It doesn't reduce load, clarify state or prevent errors.

**User delight** — Bill Scott's “interesting moments”: a by-product of smooth, low-effort flow that users barely notice mid-task, not decoration.

**Jakob's Law** — real, but used as retroactive justification.

**Element animation** — motion mistaken for polish.

try.q: A team cites the aesthetic-usability effect to ship an untested redesign. What does the effect actually say?
options: Attractive interfaces are perceived as easier
Attractive interfaces cause fewer user errors
Visual quality predicts task completion rates
Users forgive problems in products they find beautiful
try.explain: Perception is not performance: it doesn't reduce load, clarify state or prevent errors.

right.label: Rule of thumb
items: Only on user action, to show state

learn.title: Nudging, gamification, synthetic users
learn.text:
**Nudging** — fine when it helps the user; the test is “would the user choose this if they understood it?” Pushing the business goal is not a nudge.

**Gamification** — points and streaks layered onto work that is still hard.

**Synthetic users** — plausible text instead of behaviour.

None of these ideas is bad. Their **shortcut versions** are how teams ship friction with a straight face.

try.q: What is Calabro's test for whether a nudge is honest?
options: Would the user choose this if they understood it?
Does it measurably increase conversion?
Is it reversible within the same session?
Has it been approved by the legal team?
try.explain: If the answer is no, it is pushing the business goal, not nudging.

learn.title: The rule of thumb for animation
learn.text:
Element-level animation earns its place only when it is triggered **by the user** and communicates a **state change**.

That is the same test as the full article on motion: if the user didn't trigger it, it probably shouldn't move.

try.q: Which animation passes the rule of thumb?
options: A row collapsing when the user clicks it
A hero image panning on page load
A pulsing badge on a new feature
An auto-advancing tutorial overlay
try.explain: User-triggered, and it shows a state change.

test.q: What do all the ideas on Calabro's list have in common?
options: Each is real but gets used as a shortcut
Each was disproved by later research
Each comes from marketing rather than UX
Each applies only to consumer products
test.explain: “None of these ideas is bad. Their shortcut versions are how teams ship friction with a straight face.”

test.q: Whose concept of “interesting moments” does Calabro use for delight?
options: Bill Scott's
Don Norman's
Jakob Nielsen's
Kurosu and Kashimura's
test.explain: Delight is a by-product of low-effort flow.

test.q: What did the original aesthetic-usability research note about the effect?
options: It is modest and varies across cultures
It disappears in expert users
It is strongest in mobile interfaces
It only applies to first impressions of a brand
test.explain: Which is rather less than the way it gets quoted.

test.q: How is Jakob's Law misused, according to this list?
options: As retroactive justification for a decision
To argue against all novel interactions
To justify longer onboarding tours
To defend inconsistent navigation labels
test.explain: Often by copying patterns from companies big enough to train users into them.

test.q: What is wrong with gamifying a difficult workflow?
options: The work is still hard underneath the points
Users find game mechanics childish
Streaks are hard to implement accurately
It requires too much engineering effort
test.explain: Decoration doesn't remove effort — the rule of thumb is to remove effort first.
